Need to search first.I've written notes on 17 of the 30 verses. I ran out of search and fetch calls early, so I could only use the search-result extracts I had already collected and couldn't open any full pages. I found nothing to report for vv. 33–36, 38–39, 41, 52–53, 55–56, so they're left out. I found no Orthodox source and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for this passage. The tradition labels (Calvin Reformed, Clarke Methodist, Spurgeon Baptist, Guzik on the Pentecostal/charismatic site) follow your site list and the commentators' usual groupings.

---

**v. 30**
- Spurgeon's *Treasury of David* quotes an older writer on vv. 26–30. He sees two contrasts: "my ways" against "the way of Your precepts," and "the way of lying" against "the way of truth." Between them they teach what to avoid and what to embrace, both in how we live and in what we believe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html
- Augustine (Catholic, an early Church Father) says that choosing the way of truth and holding to God's testimonies is explained by v. 32: they describe running in the way of God's commandments. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801119.htm

**v. 31**
- Matthew Henry (Concise) says those who hold fast to God's word may pray in faith to be accepted. He reads "let me not be put to shame" as: don't let me do something that shames me, and don't reject my service. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-32.htm

**v. 32** (the verse where the traditions differ most)
- **Traditional reading.** Barnes: running means obeying eagerly and with all one's energy, not just walking. "Enlarge" means God sets the heart free from what holds it back. Selfishness and pride shrink the heart; love and hope enlarge it. Gill: running shows love, readiness and delight. God enlarges the heart with knowledge of Him, love, joy, and release from troubles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-32.htm
- **Reformed.** Calvin says the verse admits that people cannot make progress in doing good until God enlarges their hearts. The heart has no power to do this itself. Once God overcomes its hardness, it moves freely, and God supplies the strength as well as the desire. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-32.html The Geneva Bible note says the same: we cannot choose good or hold to God's word unless God makes the heart large enough to receive grace. Matthew Poole says David both accepts his duty and insists that he absolutely needs God's grace to do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-32.htm
- **Methodist.** Adam Clarke translates "because," not "when": God enlarges the heart by cleansing it and clearing the path, and the believer then runs and makes daily progress. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-32.html
- **Anglican and other readings.** Ellicott/Cambridge think "enlarge" may mean release from fears rather than wider abilities. The Book of Common Prayer psalter reads "set my heart at liberty." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-32.htm
- **Evangelical Q&A.** A Bible Hub article calls the verse "synergism": God starts the enlarging and the believer responds by running. It says this does not mean salvation by works. That framing contrasts with Calvin's. https://biblehub.com/q/Psalm_119_32_Free_will_guidance.htm A second article links the verse to the "new heart" of Ezekiel 36:26 and Philippians 2:13. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_enlarge_my_heart_spiritually.htm
- **Pentecostal/charismatic.** Guzik says the psalmist feels weak and dependent, and trusts God to make his heart bigger, stronger and steadier through His word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- **Catholic.** Augustine: "I could not run had Thou not widened my heart." The psalmist points to God's gifts, not his own merits. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801119.htm The Douay-Rheims translation puts it in the past tense: "I have run… when thou didst enlarge my heart." https://biblehub.com/catholic/psalms/119-32.htm
- **Scholarship.** The Pulpit Commentary calls the second clause ambiguous; it may mean "for thou hast enlarged my heart." Keil & Delitzsch say God widened the heart by giving the persecuted man joy in confessing his faith and confidence in hope. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-32.htm

**v. 37**
- Precept Austin points out the personal pronouns. David knew the grip of worthless sights (Bathsheba), and today the Spirit gives the desire and power to look away (Philippians 2:13). It quotes Spurgeon: asking God to turn his eyes doesn't make the psalmist passive. It confesses he is helpless without grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- Augustine says the chief "vanity" is the love of human praise: deeds done for glory among people bring an empty reward. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801119.htm

**v. 40**
- Guzik: another prayer for revival, from a heart that loves God's precepts, asking to be made alive in God's righteousness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/

**v. 42**
- GotQuestions lists this verse among the psalm's references to taunts and slander, part of its theme of the believer suffering persecution. https://www.gotquestions.org/Psalm-119.html
- The Bridgeway commentary says God's word assures him of salvation, and that gives him courage to answer those who mock him (vv. 41–43). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-45.html

**v. 43**
- Augustine, quoted by Spurgeon, takes "utterly" to mean: even if I fall through weakness and fail to confess the word, don't leave me there, but restore me. He gives Peter as the example. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tod/psalms-119.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: he prays not to be brought to the point where he can no longer witness to the truth. His confidence rests on God's judgments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-45.htm

**v. 44**
- David Dickson, quoted by Spurgeon: the Lord keeping the heart in faith is what makes us persevere. "So shall I keep" means "this will encourage me and enable me." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html

**v. 45**
- **Traditional reading.** Barnes: the Hebrew means wide or spacious. Luther translated it "freely"; the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) has "in a broad place." The psalmist would be free of evil passions. Gill: this is not freedom to do as one likes but gospel liberty under the Spirit, walking in God's "exceeding broad" law. Matthew Henry: serving sin is slavery and serving God is liberty. Pulpit: the word means an open city square, and he obeys from desire, not compulsion. Keil & Delitzsch: walking courageously, without being intimidated, from an inner freedom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-45.htm
- **Reformed.** Calvin: whoever obeys God has a calm mind, and finds the way through difficulties by leaving the outcome to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-45.html

**v. 46**
- **Lutheran.** Keil & Delitzsch say the Latin Vulgate's wording of this verse became the motto of the Augsburg Confession. They add that the Vulgate's past-tense reading doesn't match the Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-45.htm
- Benson: kings usually scorn godly talk, yet he will speak anyway. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-45.htm
- An older writer quoted by Spurgeon says the verse warns against two faults: staying silent too much and talking uselessly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html

**v. 47**
- Charles Bridges, quoted by Spurgeon: it is poor comfort to talk well about God's ways while one's own heart is cold; the believer longs for real delight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html
- Matthew Henry (Concise): don't just agree that God's law is good; take pleasure in it as good for you. Benson: other rulers delight in worldly glory, but God's law is his delight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-45.htm

**v. 48**
- Keil & Delitzsch: lifting the hands shows eager longing, as in prayer. The repeated "which I love" may be a copying error. Benson: the hands are lifted to receive the precepts by faith and love, and to carry them out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-45.htm

**v. 49**
- Augustine: "Remember" doesn't mean God forgets. It is the language of someone asking for what was promised: "fulfil Your promise to Your servant." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801119.htm

**v. 50**
- The NET Bible notes say the hope that the promise creates brings comfort because the promise revives him. Another possible reading of the grammar: "this" is the promise's power to revive. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 51**
- NET note: the Hebrew is literally "scoff at me to excess." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=119

**v. 54**
- NET note: some take the Hebrew word *magor* to mean a temporary home, so the psalmist is a foreign resident (compare v. 19). But the word can also mean any dwelling place, so NET translates "in the house where I live." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Psa&chapter=119&verse=54

**v. 57**
- **Baptist.** Spurgeon's sermon says grace comes first and the resolve to obey grows out of it. Earning privilege by duty is the law; privilege leading to obedience is the gospel. The Lord must be your portion before you can keep His words, and no one can earn God. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons23.xlii.html In the *Treasury of David*, Spurgeon calls it a broken, wondering exclamation: "My portion, O Lord!" Like the Levites, David took God as his share. An older writer quoted there passes on Luther's advice to answer temptation with "I am a Christian," and suggests "The Lord is my portion" as the answer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_057-064.cfm
- **Reformed.** Calvin: others may chase whatever good they imagine; his portion is giving himself completely to God's word. **Methodist.** Clarke reads vv. 57–60 as the stages of grace in the heart, from first light to fullness. Gill also gives an alternative reading: "This I said to many, perhaps they will keep thy words." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-57.html
- The Geneva note: keeping God's law is an inheritance and great gain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-57.htm
- **Catholic.** The Douay-Rheims reads "O Lord, my portion, I have said, I would keep thy law." https://biblehub.com/catholic/psalms/119-57.htm

**v. 58**
- Spurgeon: the psalmist talks of favour and mercy and never of merit. He asks rather than demands, even though God is already his portion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-119.html
- Guzik: he asks for mercy not as a right, but because God's word promises it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/

**v. 59**
- Spurgeon's preaching outline groups vv. 58–60 as the Lord being "heartily sought." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_057-064.cfm
- Clarke includes this verse in the stages of grace he sees in vv. 57–60. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-57.html

---

To fill the gaps, the next step is to open each verse's pages on biblehub.com/commentaries (for example, 119-36 and 119-53) and Spurgeon's *Treasury of David* sections for vv. 33–40, 41–48 and 49–56. I can do that if you want.
